statement: In people who use drugs given test strips or colour test kits to check their own drugs, handing out kits compared with not handing them out: the evidence is insufficient to say whether it causes harm, for example through false reassurance after a negative result, or reduces harm, and the question is disputed. No study read compared people given kits with people not given them on harm or overdose. What was measured shows few riskier responses: in a British Columbia take-home programme, 6 of 336 survey answers (2 in 100) described using alone or using more or faster after a strip showed fentanyl, in answer to standard questions, and the one study comparing overdoses in people who did and did not use strips found no clear difference, in an imprecise estimate (risk ratio 1.20, 95% CI 0.70 to 2.06). But no study read reports what people did after a negative result (the take-home programme asked and did not report it); a scoping review relays people believing that a negative strip means xylazine or that a darker line means stronger fentanyl, one person saying a negative result would mean using a little more, and strips missing carfentanil and other drugs; and at home, strips showed fentanyl in 73 of 265 methamphetamine samples (28 in 100) and 16 of 93 cocaine samples (17 in 100), against 5 of 97 (5 in 100) and 1 of 92 (1 in 100) tested by staff on site, which the authors think more likely reflects how the tests were done than a different supply. Two critiques argue, without data, that frequent positive results without ill effects could breed complacency, that people who want fentanyl may seek a positive result, and that a colour test showing MDMA may be read as meaning a pill is safe; one of them still supports handing out strips with guidance and naloxone. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
plain: No study has measured whether handing out test kits causes harm. When people were asked, few said they took more risks after a strip showed fentanyl (about 2 in 100 answers), and one study found no clear difference in overdoses. But no study reported what people did after a strip showed no fentanyl, some people misread strips, strips miss some drugs, and at home they showed fentanyl in stimulants far more often than staff found. Critics worry that a negative result may make people feel safe when they are not; this has not been measured.
population: People who use drugs given fentanyl test strips (North America, 2017–2023) or colour test kits for ecstasy (Europe, as discussed in 2001), and published critiques of self-testing
exposure: Handing out test kits for people to test their own drugs
comparator: Not handing out kits (no study read made this comparison directly)
outcome: Harms: riskier use after a result, false reassurance after a negative or reassuring result, complacency, misreading results; and overdose
magnitude: Klaire: riskier responses 6/336 answers (1.8%; Wilson 0.8–3.8%, editors' calculation), 1 using more or faster and 5 using alone; responses to a negative result asked but not reported; take-home against on-site positivity, crystal methamphetamine 73/265 (27.6%) against 5/97 (5.2%), difference 22.4 points (14.8–30.1), cocaine 16/93 (17.2%) against 1/92 (1.1%), 16.1 (7.1–25.1). Vickers-Smith: nonfatal overdose adjusted RR 1.20 (0.70–2.06), unadjusted 2.06 (1.09–3.89); composite risk-reduction score 0.86 points higher (0.34–1.38) on 0–15. Kutscher (relayed): riskier use in two studies; difficulty interpreting results 3% to almost 34%. No study reports behaviour after a negative result.

evidence.locator: Methods › Survey tools and testing kits, 2nd paragraph (p. 3); Results, 8th paragraph (p. 4)
evidence.extracted: Each participant was asked about actions in response to both a positive and a negative result, in standard questions not based on their own results; for a positive result, 6 of 336 answers (1.8%) reported a riskier response (1 using more or more quickly, 5 using alone) and 217 (64.6%) no change. Editors' observation: responses to a negative result are not reported in the Results. Editors' calculation: 6 of 336 is 1.8% (Wilson 95% CI 0.8–3.8%).

Strips showed fentanyl in 73 of 265 crystal methamphetamine samples tested at home (27.6%) against 5 of 97 tested on site by trained staff (5.2%), and in 16 of 93 cocaine samples (17.2%) against 1 of 92 (1.1%); different samples were tested, nothing was confirmed in a laboratory, and the study was not powered for stimulants. The authors think how the tests were done a more likely explanation than a differently contaminated supply, citing reports of false positives with stimulants.

evidence.locator: Results › Overdose Risk Reduction Behaviors › Mean Daily Composite Score; Mean Daily Probability of Each Behavior; Mean Daily Risk of Self-Reported Nonfatal Overdose; Table 3
evidence.extracted: Over four weeks, people who used strips at baseline had an adjusted composite risk-reduction score 0.86 points higher (95% CI 0.34–1.38) on a 0–15 scale, and reported more naloxone nearby (RR 1.10, 1.04–1.18), testing the strength of drugs before use (1.41, 1.24–1.61), asking someone to check on them (1.26, 1.10–1.45) and throwing out bad or unexpected drugs (1.50, 1.12–2.01), but less use by routes other than injection (0.86, 0.79–0.94); self-reported nonfatal overdose: adjusted RR 1.20 (0.70–2.06), unadjusted 2.06 (1.09–3.89).
evidence.source_read: Publisher full text (HTML), https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamanetworkopen/fullarticle/2833888, searched in the saved page text (scratchpad/vickers_page.txt)

evidence.locator: Results › FTS accuracy and reliability, 1st paragraph; Acceptability of FTS use by community › Limitations of FTS in an evolving drug supply, 3rd paragraph (AM p. 4); Feasibility of FTS Use › Ease of use, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (AM p. 5); Behavior Change from FTS Results, 7th paragraph (AM p. 7)
evidence.extracted: As relayed (studies not appraised): carfentanil, norcarfentanil and norfentanyl test negative on strips; strips give no information on xylazine, synthetic cannabinoids, phenacetin, levamisole or etizolam; difficulty interpreting results ranged from 3% to almost 34%; some people believed that the intensity of the line shows how pure the fentanyl is, or that a negative strip indicates xylazine (and a positive one excludes it); a few participants in two studies said they use or would use strips to use more or faster, one saying a negative result would mean doing a little more, and in one study six participants (1.8%) reported riskier behaviour after a positive result.

evidence.locator: Results › Behavior Change from FTS Results, 4th and 5th paragraphs; Overdose related outcomes after FTS use, 1st to 4th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: As relayed: a median of 55% (range 23–75%) reported any positive behaviour change across seven studies, while some used drugs as usual after a positive result because of withdrawal, tolerance, doubt about the result or wanting fentanyl. Only two of the 91 articles discuss overdose-related outcomes, neither with a control group; in the vending-machine evaluation, county overdose deaths fell by about 10% while Ohio's rose by about 5%, with naloxone dispensed by the same machine; the review concludes that only limited data suggest strip use decreases overdose rates or mortality.

To limit the risk from false negatives, participants were told that fentanyl or its analogues may be present despite a negative strip and were instructed to practise overdose prevention whatever the result. Of the 31 with a positive result, 45% used smaller amounts, 42% went slower and 39% used with someone else around (self-report). Editors' observation: what participants did after a negative result is not reported.

Before use, staff recorded an intention to reduce the dose after 142 of 391 fentanyl-positive checks (36.3%) against 7 of 122 negative checks (5.7%), and an intention to dispose of the drug after 50 of 436 positive checks (11.5%); what people then did was not recorded.
evidence.located_by: AI reader 140 (first reader), from AI reader 137's study card

evidence.locator: Results › Individual behavioural outcomes, 1st paragraph (p. 105); Pilot limitations and future directions, 3rd paragraph (p. 106)
evidence.extracted: 30 of 45 clients (66.7%) whose sample did not match what it was sold as handed over further substances for police destruction, observed by the service. Possible unintended consequences, such as displacement to other drugs including alcohol (raised anecdotally by some clients after their results), were not monitored; the author argues that, as clients had already acquired the substances they submitted, testing is more likely to deter than to stimulate drug use at the festival (an argument, not a measurement).

evidence.locator: Testing for fentanyl and fentanyl analogues, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: At Insite, 86% of all samples and 90% of 'heroin' samples tested positive (as cited from Vancouver Coastal Health), possibly an overestimate because 62% of checks were made after use; the authors argue that frequent positive results without ill effects, particularly after use, can lead to complacency and limit risk reduction (no data given), and cite a Health Canada warning that the strips were not designed for consumers to test dissolved drugs, which could lead to false negatives.

evidence.locator: What do we need to know about fentanyl self-testing? › Effect, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Acceptability, 2nd paragraph (p. 34); Do we know enough?, 3rd paragraph (p. 35)
evidence.extracted: Hypotheses without data: where fentanyl is wanted, a positive result may be sought or fail to deter use, particularly in withdrawal; strips give no amount; contaminated spoons may give positives; it is unclear whether a test that routinely shows non-fatal fentanyl will promote complacency; strips may not reach the people most at risk. The authors nonetheless support handing out strips with clear guidance on reading results, alongside low-threshold naloxone and within broader harm-reduction services, which they say may mitigate the risk of false negatives and complacency.

evidence.locator: The usefulness of pill testing, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (p. 1145); For harm reduction purposes, 1st paragraph (pp. 1145–1146)
evidence.extracted: The authors call false reassurance, from reading a pill in which MDMA has been identified as a 'safe' pill, a particular worry; colour tests give no strength and cannot tell isomers apart. They state that behaviour change after pill testing is not substantiated, citing a survey of over 1000 people at UK clubs (the first author's study) in which 40% said they would take more if pills were thought to have improved, and a Dutch study (1997) finding testing facilities unrelated to drug use.

evidence.locator: Results › Influence of DCS on behaviour of PWUD, 8th paragraph; Results › Study quality
evidence.extracted: In three European cross-sectional studies, clients of drug checking services reported more frequent ecstasy use than people at the same events who did not use the services, while in the multi-country study how often people used the services was negatively correlated with how often they used ecstasy and with unsafe party behaviour; the 13 appraised articles were all judged of relatively poor quality.

risk_of_bias.note: Self-reports and answers to standard questions from people who chose to test; the two critiques are narrative and select their sources (editors' checklist: high); no study compared people given kits with people not given them on harm.

inconsistency.note: The measured data do not conflict with one another; the dispute is between those data and the critiques' reasoning, which the debate box sets out rather than rating it as inconsistency.

indirectness.note: No study measured behaviour after negative results or false reassurance itself; the colour-test arguments concern ecstasy pills around 2000.

imprecision.note: Riskier responses rest on 6 answers, and the overdose interval runs from 0.70 to 2.06.

grade.reasoning: Observational and narrative evidence, starts low; risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision each take a level: very low. Status contested: credible critiques (McGowan et al., 2018; Winstock et al., 2001) change how the early evidence is read, and the measured data lean towards benefit in what people say but show no measured benefit or harm on overdose. The claim does not rest only on narrative reviews: its measured data come from primary studies (Klaire et al., Vickers-Smith et al., Krieger et al., Karamouzian et al., Measham). Studies inside the two reviews are counted once. The accuracy of the tests themselves is rated in the test-accuracy claims, not here.

debate.question: Does handing out test strips to people who use drugs reduce harm, or can it cause harm, for example through false reassurance?
debate.evidence_yes: People who found fentanyl often said they then did things thought to lower overdose risk: of 31 young adults in Rhode Island with a positive strip, 45 in 100 said they used smaller amounts, 42 went slower and 39 used with someone else around (Krieger et al., 2018; sc_krieger_2018); at a Vancouver supervised injection site, staff recorded an intention to use less after 36 in 100 checks before use that showed fentanyl, against 6 in 100 that did not (Karamouzian et al., 2018; sc_karamouzian_2018); a scoping review relays a median of 55 in 100 reporting some safer change across seven studies (Kutscher et al., 2024; sc_kutscher_2024). At a festival where chemists tested drugs, 30 of 45 people whose drug was not as sold handed over drugs for destruction, observed by the service (Measham, 2019; sc_measham_2019). Over four weeks, people who used strips reported more risk-reduction behaviours than people who did not (adjusted difference 0.86 on a 0 to 15 score; for example naloxone nearby, risk ratio 1.10, 1.04 to 1.18) (Vickers-Smith et al., 2025; sc_vickers_smith_2025). Riskier responses were rare when asked (6 of 336 answers; Klaire et al., 2022; sc_klaire_2022), and a vending-machine evaluation relayed by the scoping review reports county overdose deaths falling by about 10% while the state's rose by about 5%. The critique most cautious about self-testing still supports handing out strips with guidance and naloxone (McGowan et al., 2018; sc_mcgowan_2018).
debate.evidence_no: No study read shows that handing out strips prevents overdose or death: the only comparison of people who used strips with people who did not found no clear difference in self-reported overdose (adjusted risk ratio 1.20, 0.70 to 2.06; unadjusted 2.06, 1.09 to 3.89) (Vickers-Smith et al., 2025), and the scoping review found only 2 of 91 studies reporting overdose outcomes, neither with a comparison group (Kutscher et al., 2024). Most answers in the take-home programme described no change after a positive result (217 of 336; Klaire et al., 2022), few people intended to throw a drug away after a positive strip at the supervised injection site (11 in 100; Karamouzian et al., 2018), and the review relays people using as usual because of withdrawal, tolerance, doubt about the result or wanting fentanyl. Strips show only whether fentanyl is there, not how much, and as relayed they miss carfentanil and say nothing about xylazine and other drugs; some people misread them (believing a negative means xylazine or a darker line means stronger fentanyl), and at home they showed fentanyl in stimulant samples about 5 and 15 times as often as staff found on site (editors' calculation, the ratio of the two shares, from Klaire et al., 2022; sc_klaire_2022). Critiques argue that a negative result may falsely reassure (a Health Canada warning about false negatives, cited by McGowan et al., 2018), that frequent positives without ill effects could breed complacency and that people who want fentanyl may seek a positive result (McGowan et al., 2018; sc_mcgowan_2018), and that a colour test showing MDMA may be read as meaning a pill is safe (Winstock et al., 2001; sc_winstock_2001), which also cites a survey in which 40 in 100 people at clubs said they would take more if pills were thought to have improved. In three European studies, people who used drug checking used ecstasy more often than people who did not (Maghsoudi et al., 2022; sc_maghsoudi_2022), which may reflect who chooses to test.
debate.neither_can_show: Whether handing out strips changes overdose or death: the sources read contain no randomized or well-controlled comparison, and people who use strips differ from those who do not (more fentanyl use and injecting, more earlier risk reduction), so comparisons between them mix testing with who tests. Whether false reassurance happens, and how often: no study read reports what people did after a negative result, and the harms in the critiques are reasoned, not measured. What people actually took after any result: apart from the festival handovers, the figures are self-reports, intentions or answers to standard questions from people who chose to test. Settings: almost all data come from North American services where fentanyl was common, and the colour-test critique concerns ecstasy pills in Europe around 2000.
debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). In the sources read, handing out test strips has not been shown either to cause harm or to prevent overdose. What people say leans towards benefit: after a positive result a minority to a majority report using less or more carefully, and riskier responses were rare when asked; but these are self-reports from people who chose to test and who already did more to lower their risk. The harms the critiques describe are plausible and unmeasured; the largest gap is what people do after a negative result, which no study read reports, although one programme asked. The strips' own limits (no amount, missed drugs, misreading, positive readings at home for stimulants) are facts about the tests, rated in the test-accuracy claims, not evidence of what people then do. The single comparison of overdose is too imprecise to rule out either a benefit or a harm.
debate.what_would_settle_it: A cluster-randomized trial or stepped roll-out of strip distribution across sites or areas, with naloxone and the same advice in both arms, recording what people do after positive and after negative results (verified where possible, for example by photographs of strips or laboratory checks of a share of samples), with overdose and death taken from emergency, hospital and death records; and studies that test the same samples at home and in a laboratory, so that how often people meet a false negative in real use is known.
